analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and its coverage, protections, and taxes in full.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in nine House committees for the entire two-year Congress with only two cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe the Affordable Care Act off the books, retroactive to the day it passed, and reverse the health care sections of the 2010 follow-up law. That means ending the marketplaces and subsidies that help people buy insurance, the Medicaid expansion, protections for people with pre-existing conditions, requirements that insurers cover essential care, and the taxes on high earners and health industries that paid for it. The bill never moved beyond being referred to committees.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main gains would go to high-income households (the ACA's 3.8% investment-income tax and other taxes on top earners would disappear) and to health industries freed from ACA taxes and coverage requirements. Insurers would shed the medical loss ratio and essential-benefits rules, though they would also lose millions of subsidized customers.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the entire Affordable Care Act, retroactive to its 2010 enactment, and restores the laws as they stood before it. [S2] [S3]

It also repeals the health care provisions of the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010, the follow-up law that added the subsidies, the Medicaid expansion financing, and the high-income Medicare tax. [S2] [S3]
Restoring pre-ACA law would eliminate the taxes the ACA placed on high-income households and on health industries such as medical devices and brand-name drugs. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people: repeal would end marketplace subsidies, the Medicaid expansion, guaranteed coverage for pre-existing conditions, required coverage of essential health benefits, dependent coverage up to age 26, and the Medicare drug coverage gap fix — all with no replacement in the bill. Millions would lose or face unaffordable coverage.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurance buyers, Medicaid patients, people with pre-existing conditions

drawbacks.text: Repeal is retroactive to 2010 with no replacement provisions at all, so every ACA coverage expansion and consumer protection ends on day one: subsidies, Medicaid expansion, guaranteed issue for pre-existing conditions, essential health benefits, and the children's coverage age limit. [S2] [S3]

Restoring the pre-ACA tax code would strip the revenue that financed the coverage expansions, ending the 3.8% tax on high earners' investment income and industry fees, shifting the cost of care for the uninsured back to hospitals, providers, and state budgets. [S2] [S3]
The bill also repeals the Medicare prescription drug coverage gap closure, so seniors would again pay full cost for drugs in the gap rather than the discounted rate the law created. [S2] [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains flow narrowly to high earners and industries through repealed taxes; the costs are broad and immediate for tens of millions of people who gained coverage or protection under the ACA. The bill offers no transition or replacement. On its terms, the costs plainly outweigh the benefits for the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to nine committees on day one and scattered across five subcommittees, and no committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Fleming introduced the bill on January 14, 2015; it was referred the same day to the Energy and Commerce Committee plus eight other committees. [S1] [S5]
Between January and April 2015, portions were referred to five subcommittees, including Health, Higher Education and Workforce Training, and Indian, Insular and Alaska Native Affairs. [S5]
No markup, hearing, or vote is recorded in the action history, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2017 with the bill still pending in committee. [S5] [S1]
Only two other members cosponsored the bill, both Republicans. [S4] [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The people who kept ACA coverage and protections — marketplace customers, Medicaid expansion enrollees, and people with pre-existing conditions — because nothing changed. Insurers also kept their expanded, subsidy-backed customer base.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Everyone who kept ACA coverage and protections

for.name: Rep. John Fleming
for.what_they_did: Introduced the full repeal bill and referred it to nine committees.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Scheduling authority — never brought the bill to the floor
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee action or floor consideration for the bill during the 114th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only support came from three Republicans; no Democrat backed a full repeal of the ACA.

industries.note: Repeal would free insurers from the medical loss ratio and essential-benefits requirements but also end the subsidies and individual mandate that brought them millions of newly insured customers. The ACA made insurers the paid channel for public coverage; this bill would have torn that arrangement out without any replacement.

Repealing the ACA and the reconciliation act's health provisions erases the 3.8% Medicare tax on high earners' investment income and other taxes aimed at upper incomes. That revenue is what funded the coverage expansions.
The ACA's 2.3% excise tax on device sales would disappear under full repeal, removing a tax the industry lobbied against for years.
Repeal ends the ACA's brand-drug fees and the mandated 50% discount seniors receive in the Medicare coverage gap, but also ends the expanded coverage that brought the industry more paying customers.

Repeal removes uncompensated-care payment adjustments hospitals received in exchange for accepting coverage cuts, while simultaneously returning them the burden of caring for a large newly uninsured population with no payment mechanism.
